web_evidence.title: Project Hail Mary — official Del Rey/Penguin sample
web_evidence.note: The authorized 49-page sample opens with sustained first-person narration by the waking protagonist, including his perceptions, actions, and internal reasoning.

web_evidence.title: Encounters with the Other in Ray Bradbury’s The Martian Chronicles and Andy Weir’s Project Hail Mary
web_evidence.note: This scholarly thesis explicitly states that Weir’s three main novels, including Project Hail Mary, are narrated in first person and analyzes the novel as a whole.

web_evidence.title: Review: Project Hail Mary
web_evidence.note: The review explicitly describes the entire book as first-person narration from Grace’s point of view, covering both the spacecraft plot and Earth flashbacks.

web_evidence.title: Review – Project Hail Mary by Andy Weir
web_evidence.note: The reviewer explicitly identifies the novel’s first-person point of view and explains that it limits readers to Grace’s insight into other characters.

Opened the official publisher sample and confirmed sustained first-person narration in the opening.
Opened a scholarly University of Oulu thesis and confirmed its whole-work statement that Project Hail Mary is narrated in first person.
Opened two independent reviews that explicitly describe the whole novel as Grace’s first-person narrative; found no credible evidence of sustained base narration in another person.

Checked Google Books, Penguin Random House catalog/interview pages, and synopsis results; these verified the edition and protagonist but were not used as person evidence because their descriptive grammar is nondiagnostic.
person_note: Ryland Grace is the participating first-person narrator throughout the controlling narrative. The input quotes repeatedly expose his base narration through first-person action, perception, and internal commentary in both the present-time spacecraft plot and past-tense remembered scenes. Dialogue-only and gnomic quotations were treated as non-base, while bare named-character actions or generic “you/we” statements were not promoted to third- or second-person evidence. The authorized opening independently demonstrates sustained first person, and whole-book scholarly and review evidence confirms that the same viewpoint controls the novel. No credible source indicates alternating or framed narration; the main limitation is that the Tier A excerpt covers only the opening, resolved by the extensive interior quote evidence and explicit whole-book sources.
